20451-the-confessions-of-artemas-quibble:
Arthur Train, a lawyer who wrote comic fiction, edited The Confessions of Artemas Quibble as the mock memoir of a shady attorney. Quibble tells his own life story with pride. The joke is that he sees nothing wrong in it.

Quibble recalls a poor childhood after his mother's marriage. A parent's odd ways left the family with little money. The boy had to wear his stepfather's worn-out clerical clothes, which may explain his later dislike of all things churchly. From that start, the confessions follow a career of tricks played on clients, courts, and the law itself.

govdocs-archive_org-NewZealandUFO_Declas:
File AIR 39/3/3 is the New Zealand Defence Force's file on unidentified flying objects, opened in 1952 and closed in 1955 in its first volumes. The file, titled Flying Saucers in the usage of the day, was declassified in September 2010. Volumes one and two are preserved here.

Reports from pilots, servicemen, and the public, with official correspondence and press clippings, fill the file in the order the Air Force kept them. New Zealand's small official saucer archive mirrors those of larger powers: curiosity, caution, and no conclusions. The release made it the southern hemisphere's counterpart to the better-known British and American UFO files.
govdocs-archive_org-mkchickwit-mksearch-:
In 1977 the CIA's mind-control programs broke into the open, and newspapers covered the revelations day by day. This file compiles OCR'd press clippings from that year on three MKULTRA subprojects: MKCHICKWIT, MKSEARCH, and MKOFTEN.

The clippings include New York Times reporting on CIA-funded research at Georgetown University, money that reached the university through the Geschickter Foundation. Read in sequence, the stories show the scandal unfolding in public: secret funding, unwitting research subjects, and a university caught in the middle. The compilation preserves the mind-control story as the press told it at the time.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ExtremistsFBIUs: An FBI routing slip circulated among senior Bureau officials, including Clyde Tolson, J. Edgar Hoover's closest aide, and Mark Felt. journal-of-a-voyage-from-okkak-on-the-co:
Benjamin Kohlmeister and George Kmoch's Journal of a Voyage tells of a mission journey along the Labrador coast. Both men were missionaries of the United Brethren, the Moravian Church. They sailed from Okkak toward Ungava Bay, west of Cape Chudleigh. Their aim was to explore the coast and visit the Esquimaux of that unknown region.

The London edition of 1814 was printed for the Brethren's Society for the Furtherance of the Gospel. That society spread the Moravian message among peoples its members called heathen. The journal records coasts, weather, and meetings with Inuit communities new to European missionaries. It stands as an early firsthand account of Labrador's far north and its people.
nasa-tm-19660007948-a-solution-for-satel:
Goddard's Dynamics and Advanced Missions group solved a neat orbital problem in this 1965 report, number DR 105. A satellite passes through shadow in each orbit. In full shadow, called umbra, it gets no sunlight at all. In partial shadow, or penumbra, it gets some. The report gives a way to compute the time spent in each state.

Shadow time decides power and heating for a satellite. Solar cells rest while batteries carry the load in darkness. The method is applied to a lunar satellite mission analysis. Mission planners could then size batteries and plan work with the shadow periods already known, rather than guessed.
nasa-tm-19660020395-feasibility-studies-:
Henry C Haller and Seymour Lieblein at Lewis Research Center studied radiators that shed a spacecraft's waste heat, in a paper for a June 1966 heat pipe meeting in New Mexico. Their design uses vapor chamber fins. A vapor chamber spreads heat evenly across a fin, so the whole fin glows with waste heat into space. The target use was Rankine cycle power plants for space.

A power plant in orbit has no air or water to carry heat away. Radiation from a hot surface is the only exit. Feasibility studies test whether a design can work at the needed size and weight. Haller and Lieblein give that test for a fin design that later space power work kept returning to.
nasa-tm-19680025171-oxygen-reclamation-f:
Joseph Weissbart, Wilson Smart, and Theodore Wydeven of Ames Research Center report oxygen reclamation from carbon dioxide in this paper. Long space missions need to recover oxygen from the carbon dioxide crews exhale. One promising method electrolyzes carbon dioxide at high temperature through a solid oxide electrolyte.

Only oxide ions can cross the solid electrolyte in an electric field. That property cleanly separates oxygen from the carbon dioxide stream. The paper reports a long-duration test of a small electrolyzer cell. Test tables track cell voltage, resistance, temperature, and gas flow over the run. Small amounts of water vapor in the feed gas acted as a catalyst for the cathode reaction.
nasa-tm-19720003678-a-thermosphere-compo:
Hasso B Niemann, Nelson W Spencer, and Gerald A Schmitt of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in July 1971, numbered X-621-71-300. It reports a measurement of atomic oxygen high in the atmosphere. Their instrument was a quadrupole mass spectrometer with a special ion source. It flew in the Thermosphere Probe. The side energy focusing design sharpened what the instrument could measure.

The team measured atomic oxygen between one hundred thirty and two hundred forty kilometers up. The ion source design raised the oxygen share among measured particles. That boost made the faint oxygen signal easier to read accurately. Atomic oxygen eats at spacecraft surfaces in low orbit. Knowing its amount by height helps predict satellite drag and decay.
podcast-joerogan-JtbGgSwuE_U:
Canadian politician Pierre Poilievre joins Joe Rogan for episode 2470. Poilievre leads Canada's Conservatives with a sharp, populist style. His plain talk on costs won him a huge base.

Rogan asks how Canada reached its current strain on housing and pay. Poilievre blames big government and pledges common sense. The talk crosses the border with ease, since both nations share gripes. The episode gives American listeners a northern leader in full. It suits the political and the curious about a neighbor in flux. Plain speech is his weapon and his brand.

the-gentleman-of-fifty-and-the-damsel-of:
George Meredith left The Gentleman of Fifty and the Damsel of Nineteen as an early fragment, never finished. A narrator tells the tale as he walks by a river near Ickleworth Bridge.

Rounding a bend, the narrator finds bathers in the bright water below the vicar's terrace steps. To his shock the bathers are the vicar himself and his portly wife, both in full dress, standing waist deep and chatting as calmly as at tea. The vicar recites Greek verse to the sun while his wife fights her ballooning skirts. Meredith turns a droll scene into a study of an absent-minded scholar and the young watcher's own sly heart.
